newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn wants to tap utilities in tax reform.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn wants to tap utilities in tax reform.

text.p: The German parliament's finance committee agreed changes to tax reforms on Friday, singling out power utilities as cash cows to help Bonn to meet borrowing targets next year for joining European economic monetary union (EMU).

Changes pushed through by Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) on the committee will scrap tax breaks on reserves built up by energy companies to pay for closing down nuclear power plants, raising four billion marks ($2.3 billion) next year.
New limits on the tax write-offs which companies can take for losses would raise an extra 1.6 billion marks, finance committee chairman Carl-Ludwig Thiele told a news conference.
"With this tax reform tax cuts will start to take effect in 1998," said Thiele, a member of the FDP which is the junior partner of the CDU/CSU in the coalition government.
Taxpayers would still end up a net 1.2 billion marks better off next year, he added.

Passage through the committee stage marks the latest step on a tortuous path for Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bumper tax reform. It is planned to take effect in two stages, with major income tax cuts starting in 1999.

The FDP recorded a victory in its tax-cutting drive by ensuring that the solidarity income tax surcharge -- raised to finance the rebuilding of east Germany -- is cut by two points to 5.5 percent next year.
But the price of that victory was the new revenue-boosting changes -- leaving Waigel still struggling to find over 30 billion marks to close gaps in the 1998 budget.
Waigel has to cut the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, a target for countries wanting to join the single European currency.

The Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, will hold the second and third readings on the tax reforms on June 26. After passing they will go to the Bundesrat, the upper house, where the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have a blocking majority.
Thiele said the changes agreed in committee would be positive for SPD-led states, adding that he could not imagine their leaders blocking the reforms in the Bundesrat.
The tax reforms would leave a financing shortage of 44.9 billion marks for the combined federal, state and local budgets in 1999, according to Finance Ministry projections.
That would be partly offset by a likely increase in indirect taxes, said Gerda Hasselfeldt, finance spokeswoman for the CDU/CSU parliamentary group.
Opposition parties poured scorn on the latest changes to the tax reforms, saying the coalition was being irresponsible and evasive on how direct tax cuts would be counter-financed.

"The coalition still refuses to give any information on how it will plug that gap," said Christine Scheel, finance spokeswoman of the Greens party said in a statement. "We can expect an increase in value-added tax by 1999 at the latest."
SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said: "A tax reform which drives the state into a crisis is not a real reform, and burdens workers, families and businesses."
The committee's plan also drew fire from energy providers who threatened legal action against taxing the billions of marks set aside for closing atomic power plants in the future.
"We will never accept that," said a spokesman for Essen-based RWE AG, which had 15.5 billion marks in fiscal 1995/96 reserved for such purposes.
Bayernwerk, part of the VIAG group, also said it was considering a legal protest. The company has set aside 8.4 billion marks to dispose of nuclear fuel rods and demolish its nuclear installations.
Coalition finance experts said the key elements of the reform -- cuts in income and corporate taxes combined with scrapping myriad tax exemptions -- had remained intact.
But the coalition put off plans to slap a three percent tax on life insurance policies and to halve the tax-free allowance on savings interest to 1999.
-- Bonn Newsroom, +49-228 26097150 ($ = 1.725 German Marks)
